summary: How vitamin D, PTH, calcitonin, and FGF23 keep calcium and phosphate in range, how muscle switches fuels as exercise goes on, and which minerals and cofactors bone and muscle depend on. Exam questions pair a lab pattern or an exercise history with the enzyme or hormone step that explains it, such as McArdle disease versus CPT II deficiency.

points: Skin: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3); diet adds D2 and D3
Liver: 25-hydroxylase makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol), the main circulating and storage form
Kidney proximal tubule: 1-alpha-hydroxylase makes 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), the active hormone
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D measures status: long half-life (weeks), loosely regulated, reflects skin plus diet supply
Calcitriol has a half-life of hours and is tightly controlled, so it can look normal even in deficiency
1-alpha-hydroxylase is turned up by PTH and low phosphate, and turned down by FGF23 and calcitriol itself
notes.why: Vitamin D is a prohormone that needs two hydroxylations before it can bind the vitamin D receptor, a nuclear receptor that changes gene transcription. The liver step is driven by substrate supply and is barely regulated, so 25-hydroxyvitamin D rises and falls with intake and sun exposure and is the right test of body stores. The kidney step is the control point, switched on by PTH and low phosphate and switched off by FGF23 and calcitriol. In deficiency, the rise in PTH drives 1-alpha-hydroxylase hard, which is why calcitriol can stay normal or even high while stores run low.

points: Low ionized calcium is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid chief cells, which then release PTH
PTH acts on osteoblasts (they carry the PTH receptor), which raise RANKL and lower OPG, so osteoclasts resorb bone
PTH increases calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and blocks phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Calcitriol raises gut absorption of both calcium and phosphate
Calcitonin from thyroid C cells inhibits osteoclasts; minor role in adult calcium balance
FGF23 from osteocytes rises with high phosphate or calcitriol, causes phosphaturia, and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase
Osteoprotegerin (OPG) from osteoblasts is a decoy receptor that binds RANKL and limits osteoclast activation
notes.why: PTH raises serum calcium within minutes through the kidney and over hours to days through bone, and in bone it works indirectly because osteoclasts lack the PTH receptor. Osteoblasts relay the signal: more RANKL and less OPG means more RANK activation on osteoclast precursors. PTH makes the kidney excrete phosphate so that calcium released from bone does not precipitate with phosphate. FGF23 is the phosphate-lowering counterweight, removing phosphate through the kidney and cutting calcitriol so the gut absorbs less.

points: First seconds: stored ATP plus phosphocreatine; creatine kinase moves phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP
Up to about 2 minutes of hard effort: anaerobic glycolysis of muscle glycogen to lactate
Longer effort: oxidative metabolism of glucose, then a rising share from fatty acid beta-oxidation
Cori cycle: muscle lactate goes to the liver, becomes glucose by gluconeogenesis, and returns to muscle (net cost 4 ATP)
Creatinine forms nonenzymatically from creatine and phosphocreatine at a steady daily rate, so it tracks muscle mass
notes.why: Each energy system trades speed for capacity. Phosphocreatine regenerates ATP in a single enzymatic step, so it is the fastest source but runs out within about 10 seconds of maximal effort. Anaerobic glycolysis yields only 2 ATP per glucose (3 per glucose unit taken from glycogen) but runs fast without oxygen, regenerating NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate, while oxidative phosphorylation yields far more ATP and dominates sustained exercise. In the Cori cycle the liver spends 6 ATP to rebuild one glucose from 2 lactate while muscle gains only 2, giving the net cost of 4 ATP.

points: McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V): autosomal recessive loss of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase)
McArdle: cramps and fatigue in brief intense exercise, myoglobinuria, high CK, blood lactate fails to rise with exercise
McArdle second wind: after about 10 minutes, blood flow brings glucose and fatty acids and the patient can continue
Carnitine shuttle: CPT I on the outer membrane, translocase, CPT II on the inner membrane move long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria
CPT II deficiency: weakness, muscle pain, and rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria after prolonged exercise, fasting, cold, or illness
notes.why: The timing of symptoms points to the defective pathway. Brief intense exercise depends on muscle glycogenolysis, so loss of myophosphorylase leaves the fiber without fuel early, and during ischemic forearm exercise lactate fails to rise while ammonia still rises. Prolonged exercise, fasting, and cold depend on long-chain fatty acid oxidation, so CPT II deficiency fails late, after glycogen is used up. In both disorders the ATP-starved fiber cannot run its ion pumps or keep its membrane intact, so it breaks down and releases CK and myoglobin.

points: Bone mineral is calcium hydroxyapatite, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2, laid down on type I collagen
Magnesium is needed for PTH secretion and action; severe hypomagnesemia causes hypocalcemia that persists until magnesium is replaced
Copper is the cofactor for lysyl oxidase, which cross-links collagen and elastin
Vitamin K drives gamma-carboxylation of glutamate on osteocalcin so it can bind calcium in bone matrix
Vitamin C drives prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation of collagen (see scurvy)
notes.why: Bone strength depends on a correctly built, cross-linked collagen scaffold and on mineral deposited onto it. Vitamin C and copper both act on collagen after translation: hydroxylation of proline stabilizes the triple helix through hydrogen bonds, and lysyl oxidase forms covalent cross-links between collagen molecules outside the cell. Severe hypomagnesemia impairs PTH release and causes end-organ resistance to PTH, so calcium stays low until magnesium is restored. Vitamin K-dependent carboxylation adds a second carboxyl group to glutamate residues, creating the calcium-binding sites osteocalcin needs to bind hydroxyapatite.

summary: The genes that build the skeleton and muscle, and what happens when they fail: transcription factor defects, collagen and dystrophin mutations, repeat expansions, mitochondrial inheritance, and the tumor suppressor and fusion gene changes behind bone sarcomas. Exam questions ask you to predict severity from the type of mutation and to name the inheritance pattern from a pedigree or family history.

points: RUNX2 is the master switch for osteoblast differentiation
RUNX2 haploinsufficiency (autosomal dominant) causes cleidocranial dysplasia: absent or small clavicles, open fontanelles, delayed suture closure, extra teeth
SOX9 drives chondrocyte differentiation from mesenchyme
HOX genes give each body segment its identity along the head to tail axis; mutations put structures in the wrong place (for example HOXD13 synpolydactyly)
notes.why: Transcription factors sit at the top of differentiation cascades, so losing one copy can change a whole tissue. RUNX2 turns mesenchymal cells into osteoblasts; with half the normal dose, membranous bones such as the clavicle and skull vault ossify poorly, and tooth development is disturbed as well. SOX9 acts on the cartilage path, and its haploinsufficiency causes campomelic dysplasia. HOX genes are expressed in a nested order along the body axis, so a mutation changes the positional identity of a segment while the tissue types stay normal.

points: Achondroplasia: FGFR3 gain-of-function mutation keeps the receptor active and slows chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate
Endochondral bone is short (limbs) while membranous bone is normal, so the head is large and the trunk near normal
Most achondroplasia cases are new autosomal dominant mutations linked to advanced paternal age
Type I collagen is two alpha-1 chains (COL1A1) and one alpha-2 chain (COL1A2), with glycine at every third residue
Glycine substitution: the bad chain enters many triple helices (3 of 4 when COL1A1 is hit) and spoils them (dominant negative), giving severe OI types II to IV
Null allele: no bad chain is made, only half the normal amount of collagen, giving mild OI type I (blue sclerae, fractures, hearing loss)
notes.why: FGFR3 signaling normally restrains chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy, so a constitutively active receptor shortens bones that grow through a cartilage model. Membranous ossification skips the cartilage stage, which is why the skull vault and trunk width are spared. In osteogenesis imperfecta the severity depends on what reaches the triple helix: a mutant chain that is made and incorporated spoils every helix it enters, while a null allele only lowers the amount of normal collagen. Glycine is required at every third position because it is the only residue small enough to fit in the crowded center of the helix.

points: DMD gene (Xp21) is the largest human gene, a big target, so about one third of cases are new mutations
Frameshift deletion leads to an early stop codon and no dystrophin: Duchenne, onset by about age 5, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy
In-frame deletion leaves a shorter, partly working dystrophin: Becker, later onset, slower course
Severity follows the reading frame, regardless of deletion size
Dystrophin anchors actin to the dystroglycan complex and extracellular matrix; without it the sarcolemma tears with contraction
notes.why: The genetic code is read in triplets, so a deletion whose size is not a multiple of three shifts every downstream codon and soon creates a premature stop codon. The faulty transcript is destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay, and no functional dystrophin is made, giving Duchenne. An in-frame deletion removes part of the central rod domain but keeps the ends that bind actin and the dystroglycan complex, so a shorter working protein gives Becker. Without that link, contraction tears the sarcolemma, calcium floods in, and fibers necrose and are replaced by fat and fibrous tissue.

points: Myotonic dystrophy type 1: autosomal dominant CTG expansion in the DMPK gene, toxic RNA disrupts splicing
Anticipation: the repeat grows each generation; maternal transmission can cause a severe congenital form
Features: myotonia (slow grip release), distal weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy, cardiac conduction block
Mitochondrial DNA comes only from the mother: all children of an affected mother can be affected, none from an affected father
Heteroplasmy: cells carry a mix of normal and mutant mtDNA, so severity varies widely within a family
Ragged red fibers on modified Gomori trichrome are clumps of abnormal mitochondria under the sarcolemma (MERRF, MELAS)
notes.why: In myotonic dystrophy, the expanded CUG repeat in DMPK RNA stays in the nucleus and traps splicing regulators such as muscleblind-like proteins. Many transcripts then keep fetal splice forms; mis-splicing of the muscle chloride channel ClC-1 lowers chloride conductance and causes myotonia, and insulin receptor mis-splicing causes insulin resistance. Mitochondria are inherited through the oocyte and segregate at random during cell division, so the share of mutant mtDNA differs between tissues and between siblings. Disease appears when that share passes a threshold, which happens first in high-energy tissues such as muscle and brain.

points: RB1 (13q14) controls the G1 to S checkpoint; a germline RB1 mutation (hereditary retinoblastoma) raises osteosarcoma risk
Germline TP53 loss (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) causes sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, leukemia, and adrenocortical carcinoma at young ages
Ewing sarcoma: t(11;22) fuses EWSR1 to FLI1, making an abnormal transcription factor
notes.why: Tumor suppressors follow Knudson's two-hit model: a person who inherits one mutant RB1 or TP53 allele needs only one somatic hit to lose the gene, which explains early, multiple, and varied tumors. Hypophosphorylated RB binds E2F and holds the cell in G1, so losing RB frees cells to enter S phase. p53 arrests the cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage, so its loss lets damaged cells keep dividing. Ewing sarcoma works through a gain of function instead: the translocation creates EWS-FLI1, an abnormal transcription factor that switches on a growth program.

summary: How nerves drive muscle: transmission at the neuromuscular junction, the stretch and tendon reflexes, and how electrolytes change excitability. Exam questions ask you to place a weakness at the nerve, the junction, or the muscle, and to separate myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, and botulism by their mechanism.

points: Action potential reaches the terminal and opens presynaptic voltage-gated (P/Q-type) calcium channels
Calcium entry triggers SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25) to fuse vesicles and release acetylcholine
Acetylcholine binds postsynaptic nicotinic receptors, ligand-gated cation channels, producing the end plate potential
The end plate potential normally exceeds threshold by a wide safety margin and fires a muscle action potential
Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline, ending the signal
notes.why: Each step is a separate drug and disease target, which is why junction disorders can be sorted by where they act. Calcium entry through P/Q-type channels couples the nerve action potential to vesicle fusion, so anything that cuts calcium entry cuts the number of quanta released. The nicotinic receptor is a nonselective cation channel, and net inward sodium current depolarizes the end plate. Normal release is several times more than needed to reach threshold, so weakness appears only when release or receptor number falls below that reserve.

points: Botulism: toxin cleaves SNARE proteins, so no acetylcholine release; descending flaccid paralysis with dilated pupils
Lambert-Eaton syndrome: antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels reduce release; often paraneoplastic with small cell lung cancer
Lambert-Eaton: proximal limb weakness that improves with repeated effort, low reflexes, dry mouth and other autonomic signs
Myasthenia gravis: antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors block them and cause complement damage
Myasthenia gravis: weakness worsens with use and late in the day, ptosis and diplopia, normal reflexes and pupils, thymus abnormalities
notes.why: Response to repeated activity separates presynaptic from postsynaptic disease. In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, repeated firing lets calcium build up in the terminal, so release rises and strength briefly improves, seen as an incremental response to high-frequency nerve stimulation. In myasthenia gravis, release falls normally with repeated firing, and with fewer receptors the end plate potential drops below threshold, so fatigue grows with use. Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at autonomic cholinergic synapses too, causing dilated pupils and dry mouth, while myasthenia antibodies target only the muscle-type nicotinic receptor, so pupils stay normal.

points: Muscle spindles lie in parallel with muscle fibers and sense length and rate of stretch
Ia afferents from spindles excite alpha motor neurons to the same muscle (monosynaptic stretch reflex) and inhibit the antagonist
Gamma motor neurons contract the spindle ends to keep it taut and set its sensitivity
Golgi tendon organs lie in series at the muscle-tendon junction and sense tension
Ib afferents act through inhibitory interneurons to relax the same muscle under high tension
Reflex roots: biceps C5 to C6, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1
notes.why: The spindle and the tendon organ report different things because of how they are mounted. Lying in parallel with extrafusal fibers, the spindle is stretched when the muscle lengthens and goes slack when it shortens, so gamma motor neurons shorten the intrafusal fibers to keep it reporting during contraction (alpha-gamma coactivation). Lying in series with the tendon, the Golgi tendon organ is loaded by active tension, and its Ib input inhibits the same muscle (autogenic inhibition). A tendon reflex therefore tests the sensory nerve, root, cord segment, motor neuron, and muscle in one maneuver.

points: Neurogenic (lower motor neuron): fasciculations, atrophy, low reflexes, often distal; CK normal or mildly high
Biopsy in denervation: grouped atrophy; after reinnervation, fiber type grouping
Spinal muscular atrophy: SMN1 deletion, anterior horn cell loss, floppy infant with tongue fasciculations
Myopathic: proximal weakness, high CK, reflexes kept until late
Type II fiber atrophy with normal CK points to disuse or corticosteroids
notes.why: Losing a motor neuron denervates all of its muscle fibers at once, so atrophic fibers appear in groups, and surviving neurons sprout to adopt orphaned fibers and convert them to their own fiber type, which produces fiber type grouping. Fasciculations are spontaneous firing of a whole motor unit from an irritable lower motor neuron. In myopathy the fiber membrane itself is damaged, so CK leaks into the blood, and reflexes persist until much of the muscle is lost. Glucocorticoids are catabolic and atrophy fast type II fibers without necrosis, so CK stays normal.

points: Hypocalcemia lowers the threshold for sodium channel opening, so nerves fire on their own: tetany, perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm
Chvostek sign: tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear twitches the face
Trousseau sign: a blood pressure cuff inflated above systolic for 3 minutes causes carpal spasm
Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes the membrane, so threshold is harder to reach: weakness and cramps
Hyperkalemia depolarizes the membrane and inactivates sodium channels: weakness and cardiac arrhythmias
notes.why: Extracellular calcium binds negative charges on the outer face of sodium channels; when calcium falls, less charge is screened, so channels open at a more negative voltage and threshold moves closer to the resting potential. Nerves then fire on their own, which is why low calcium causes tetany even though muscle contraction needs calcium. Potassium sets the resting potential: low extracellular potassium hyperpolarizes the cell and moves it away from threshold. High potassium depolarizes the cell, and sustained depolarization keeps sodium channel inactivation gates closed, so fewer channels are available and excitability falls.

summary: How the immune system attacks joints, muscle, and connective tissue: autoimmunity in rheumatoid arthritis and the connective tissue diseases, hypersensitivity types, crystal-driven innate inflammation, and arthritis after infection or vaccination. Exam questions match an autoantibody to its disease and a joint picture to its immune mechanism.

points: Genetic risk: HLA-DR4 (shared epitope); environmental risk: smoking
Peptidyl arginine deiminase converts arginine to citrulline; citrullinated peptides break tolerance
CD4 T cells (Th1, Th17) and B cells drive synovitis; anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor (IgM against the Fc of IgG) appear
TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 inflame the synovium and cause systemic symptoms
Pannus (proliferating synovium with inflammatory cells and granulation tissue) erodes cartilage
RANKL from T cells and synovial fibroblasts activates osteoclasts, giving marginal erosions and periarticular osteopenia
notes.why: Rheumatoid arthritis starts when a genetic background meets an environmental trigger. Smoking promotes citrullination of proteins in the lung, and HLA-DR4 shared-epitope molecules present citrullinated peptides well, so CD4 T cells are activated and help B cells make anti-CCP antibodies. In the joint, TNF and IL-1 stimulate synovial fibroblasts and chondrocytes to release matrix metalloproteinases that degrade cartilage, while RANKL draws osteoclasts into bone at the margins where synovium meets bare bone. IL-6 drives the hepatic acute phase response, which raises CRP and ESR and contributes to fatigue and anemia of inflammation.

points: Symmetric MCP, PIP, and wrist synovitis; DIP joints spared
Morning stiffness over 1 hour that eases with use; fatigue and low-grade fever
Ulnar deviation, swan neck (PIP hyperextension, DIP flexion), boutonniere (PIP flexion, DIP hyperextension)
Rheumatoid nodules: central fibrinoid necrosis ringed by palisading histiocytes
Felty syndrome: rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly, and neutropenia with recurrent infections
notes.why: The deformities are mechanical results of long-standing synovitis. Chronic swelling stretches and weakens capsules, ligaments, and tendon sheaths, so tendons slip off their normal line of pull and joints sublux, which at the MCP joints draws the fingers toward the ulnar side. Swan neck and boutonniere deformities follow imbalance in the finger extensor mechanism once the volar plate, central slip, or lateral bands are damaged. Morning stiffness lasting over an hour reflects active synovial inflammation and separates RA from the brief stiffness of osteoarthritis.

points: SLE arthritis is nonerosive; hand deformities can be correctable (Jaccoud arthropathy)
Systemic sclerosis: sclerodactyly, calcinosis, flexion contractures, Raynaud phenomenon
Mixed connective tissue disease: overlap of SLE, scleroderma, and myositis features with high anti-U1 RNP
notes.why: Each disease targets a different tissue, which explains its joint picture. In SLE, synovitis is driven by immune complexes and is far less proliferative than in RA, so pannus does not form and bone is not eroded, and lax ligaments give deformities that can be pushed back into place. In systemic sclerosis, fibroblasts lay down excess collagen in the skin and around joints, and small arteries show intimal proliferation and vasospasm, giving tight skin, contractures, and Raynaud phenomenon. Mixed connective tissue disease is defined by high-titer anti-U1 RNP, which is why its overlap features travel with that antibody.

points: Type II (antibody against tissue): rheumatic fever polyarthritis from anti-M protein cross-reaction (molecular mimicry)
Type II: Lambert-Eaton, where antibodies made against tumor calcium channels cross-react with nerve terminals
Type III (immune complex): SLE arthritis and nephritis
Type IV (T cell): polymyositis, with CD8 T cells killing muscle fibers
notes.why: The hypersensitivity type is defined by the effector mechanism, whatever the organ. In type II, antibody binds an antigen fixed in tissue and either destroys cells through complement and phagocytes or changes their function, as when Lambert-Eaton antibodies block calcium channels. In type III, antigen-antibody complexes deposit in vessel walls, synovium, and glomeruli, where complement activation draws in neutrophils. Type IV needs no antibody: sensitized T cells cause the injury, as CD8 T cells do when they kill muscle fibers that express MHC class I in polymyositis.

points: Gout: macrophages take up urate crystals, NLRP3 inflammasome activates caspase-1, which releases IL-1 beta and recruits neutrophils
Septic arthritis: neutrophil proteases and bacterial enzymes destroy articular cartilage within days
Reactive arthritis: HLA-B27 linked sterile arthritis 1 to 4 weeks after enteric or Chlamydia infection
Parvovirus B19 and rubella infection: symmetric small joint arthritis in adults, mostly women, that mimics rheumatoid arthritis
Rubella vaccination: transient arthralgia or arthritis, most often in adult women
notes.why: Gout shows innate immunity acting without antigen specificity: phagocytosed urate crystals are danger signals that assemble the NLRP3 inflammasome, and caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1 beta into its active form. IL-1 beta activates endothelium and draws in neutrophils, which take up more crystals and amplify the flare. Articular cartilage has no blood supply and little capacity to repair, so bacterial and neutrophil enzymes in septic arthritis cause permanent damage within days, which makes it an emergency. Reactive arthritis is sterile on culture, and the inflammation follows the host response to the earlier bacterial infection in an HLA-B27 background.

summary: The organisms that infect bone, joints, fascia, and muscle, and the virulence factors that let them do it. Exam questions give a setting (sickle cell disease, a nail through a sneaker, a deep dirty wound, a tick bite) and ask for the organism, its lab features, or the toxin behind the damage.

points: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase positive, coagulase positive
Protein A binds the Fc of IgG, blocking opsonization and phagocytosis
Surface adhesins bind collagen, fibronectin, and fibrinogen in bone and joint tissue
Biofilm on hardware and prostheses shields bacteria from antibodies and antibiotics
Most common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis; in children it seeds the metaphysis of long bones
notes.why: S. aureus succeeds in bone by sticking to matrix and evading opsonization. Its adhesins bind collagen, fibronectin, and fibrinogen exposed in bone and joints, and protein A binds IgG by the Fc end, so the antibody faces the wrong way and phagocytes cannot grab it. In children the metaphysis is seeded because capillary loops beneath the growth plate open into sinusoids where blood flow is slow. On hardware, bacteria grow slowly inside a biofilm matrix that antibodies and antibiotics penetrate poorly, so cure usually requires removing the device.

points: Gram-negative diplococci, often inside neutrophils; ferments glucose only
Pili attach to mucosa and change antigens, so immunity does not last and no vaccine exists
IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA
Disseminated infection in sexually active young adults: tenosynovitis, pustular skin lesions, migratory polyarthralgia
Or a purulent monoarthritis, often the knee; terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency raises risk
notes.why: Gonococcal virulence centers on escaping adaptive immunity. Pili and opacity proteins undergo antigenic and phase variation by gene recombination, so antibodies against one variant miss the next, and reinfection is common. Killing of Neisseria depends heavily on the membrane attack complex, which is why C5 to C9 deficiency predisposes to disseminated disease. During bacteremia, organisms reach tendon sheaths, skin, and joints to give the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, and in other patients bacteria settle in one joint and cause purulent arthritis.

points: C. perfringens: gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming rod in deep, dirty, low-oxygen wounds
Alpha toxin is a phospholipase C (lecithinase) that destroys cell membranes, causing myonecrosis and hemolysis
Gas from bacterial fermentation produces crepitus in gas gangrene
S. pyogenes: beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive
M protein resists phagocytosis and complement; hyaluronidase and streptokinase help spread along fascial planes
Pyrogenic exotoxins act as superantigens, linking MHC II to T cell receptors outside the peptide groove and causing toxic shock
notes.why: Both organisms destroy tissue mainly through secreted products. Alpha toxin hydrolyzes lecithin in cell membranes, killing muscle cells, red cells, and endothelium, and the dead tissue extends the anaerobic environment the organism needs, so infection spreads rapidly. S. pyogenes M protein binds complement regulators such as factor H to resist opsonization, and hyaluronidase and streptokinase break down connective tissue matrix and fibrin so infection tracks along fascia. Superantigens skip antigen processing and activate a large fraction of T cells (up to about 20 percent), producing a cytokine storm with shock.

points: Spirochete carried by Ixodes ticks in the northeastern and upper midwestern United States
Larvae pick up Borrelia from white-footed mice (the reservoir); nymphs transmit it to people
Transmission usually needs about 36 hours or more of tick attachment
Deer feed adult ticks and keep the tick population going but are not the bacterial reservoir
Late Lyme disease: intermittent or persistent arthritis of large joints, most often the knee
notes.why: The transmission rules follow the tick life cycle. Borrelia is rarely passed through tick eggs, so larvae acquire it from their first blood meal on infected mice and carry it into the nymph stage. Nymphs are tiny and feed in late spring and summer, often unnoticed, which makes them the main vector to people. Spirochetes in the tick midgut must multiply and migrate to the salivary glands after feeding begins, so the risk is low if the tick is removed within about 36 hours.

points: Spreads through blood from the lung to vertebral bodies, most often lower thoracic and upper lumbar (Pott disease)
Caseating granulomas destroy the anterior vertebral body, spread to the disc and next vertebra, and collapse them
Collapse makes an angular kyphosis (gibbus deformity)
Pus can track along the psoas sheath to form a psoas abscess with groin or hip pain
notes.why: Vertebral bodies are rich in red marrow with a dense arterial supply, so blood-borne bacilli lodge in the anterior body near the endplate. Caseating granulomas destroy bone and spread beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament and across the disc space to the next vertebra, and the weakened anterior column collapses into a wedge. Because the posterior elements stay intact, collapse angles the spine forward into a sharp gibbus. The psoas arises from the lumbar vertebral bodies and discs, so a cold abscess can track down its sheath to the groin.

summary: Rickets, osteomalacia, and scurvy: two problems of mineralizing bone and one of building collagen. Exam questions give a child's skeletal findings or an adult's bone pain with lab values and ask for the deficiency, its mechanism, or the risk factor behind it.

points: Osteoid is made normally but does not mineralize, leaving wide seams of soft osteoid
Cause is usually vitamin D deficiency; phosphate loss (renal wasting) does the same
Before the growth plates close it is rickets (growth plate and bone); after they close it is osteomalacia (bone only)
Low vitamin D lowers gut calcium uptake, PTH rises, PTH wastes phosphate, and low phosphate stalls mineralization
notes.why: Mineralization needs an adequate calcium-phosphate product at the osteoid surface plus osteoblast alkaline phosphatase, which breaks down pyrophosphate, an inhibitor of crystal formation. Vitamin D deficiency lowers that product in two ways: less calcium and phosphate are absorbed, and the secondary hyperparathyroidism that follows wastes phosphate in the urine. Osteoblasts keep laying down osteoid, so unmineralized seams widen. In a growing child, hypertrophic chondrocytes in the growth plate also fail to calcify and to undergo apoptosis, so the plate widens and the metaphysis flares.

notes.h: Risk factors for vitamin D deficiency
points: Limited sun exposure, high latitude, covering clothing, and darker skin (melanin blocks UVB)
Exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D supplements (breast milk is low in vitamin D)
Fat malabsorption: celiac disease, Crohn disease, cystic fibrosis, cholestasis, bariatric surgery
Liver disease (less 25-hydroxylation) and chronic kidney disease (less 1-alpha-hydroxylation)
Anticonvulsants such as phenytoin, phenobarbital, and carbamazepine speed vitamin D breakdown
notes.why: Each risk factor removes one step of supply or activation. Melanin, sunscreen, clothing, and high latitude reduce the UVB that reaches 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin. Vitamin D is fat soluble and is absorbed in micelles, so any cause of fat malabsorption lowers dietary uptake. Liver and kidney disease reduce the two hydroxylation steps, and enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants increase hepatic cytochrome P450 breakdown of vitamin D to inactive metabolites.

points: Diffuse bone pain and tenderness, proximal muscle weakness, waddling gait, fractures
Looser zones (pseudofractures): thin lucent bands across the cortex at the femoral neck, pubic rami, ribs, and scapula
Labs: calcium low or normal, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase high, PTH high, 25-hydroxyvitamin D low
notes.why: Osteomalacia softens bone without necessarily reducing its amount, so the skeleton bends and cracks under load. Looser zones are insufficiency fractures filled with unmineralized osteoid, which is why they appear at high-stress sites and run perpendicular to the cortex. Alkaline phosphatase rises because osteoblasts are highly active, and the lab pattern follows from secondary hyperparathyroidism: PTH holds calcium near normal at the cost of low phosphate. Proximal weakness reflects the role of vitamin D and phosphate in normal muscle function.

points: Craniotabes (soft skull), frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure

notes.why: Rickets is the growth plate form of the same defect, so findings cluster where bone grows fastest. Unmineralized cartilage and osteoid pile up at the metaphysis, which widens the wrists and costochondral junctions and produces the cupped, frayed edge on radiographs. Soft bone bends under load, so the legs bow once the child walks and the infant skull yields to pressure. In X-linked hypophosphatemia, a PHEX mutation raises FGF23, which wastes phosphate in the urine and blocks 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so calcitriol stays low despite hypophosphatemia that would normally raise it.

points: Vitamin C is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase in collagen synthesis
Underhydroxylated chains cannot form stable triple helices and are degraded, leaving weak vessels and scars
Perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, easy bruising, hemarthrosis, poor wound healing
Children: painful subperiosteal hemorrhage, refusal to walk, and leg tenderness
Risks: diets without fruit and vegetables, alcohol use disorder, older adults living alone, very restricted diets
notes.why: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases are iron-containing enzymes that need ascorbate to keep their iron in the ferrous state. Hydroxyproline forms hydrogen bonds that hold the triple helix together at body temperature, so underhydroxylated procollagen is unstable and is degraded instead of secreted, and too little hydroxylysine leaves fewer cross-links. Vessel walls and their supporting tissue weaken, so capillaries bleed into skin, gums, joints, and beneath the periosteum. Collagen is also the framework of osteoid, so in children new bone formation slows.

summary: The inflammatory and overuse disorders of joints, tendons, bursae, and muscle: spondyloarthropathies, crystal arthritis, myositis, polymyalgia rheumatica, fibromyalgia, bursitis, and tendinopathy. Exam questions turn on a few sharp clues, such as crystal shape, which joints are involved, whether CK is high, and which HLA type or infection came first.

points: Ankylosing spondylitis: HLA-B27, young men, enthesitis and bilateral sacroiliitis
AS back pain is worse in the morning and with rest, better with exercise; chest expansion and lumbar flexion fall
Syndesmophytes bridge vertebrae into a bamboo spine
AS complications: anterior uveitis, aortitis with aortic regurgitation, restrictive lung disease, fractures of the fused spine
Reactive arthritis: HLA-B27, 1 to 4 weeks after Chlamydia trachomatis or Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter; joint fluid sterile
Reactive arthritis: asymmetric leg arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis, enthesitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum
Psoriatic arthritis: DIP involvement, dactylitis (sausage digits), nail pitting, pencil-in-cup deformity; axial disease linked to HLA-B27
notes.why: HLA-B27 links these diseases, and their shared target is the enthesis, where tendon, ligament, or capsule inserts into bone. Enthesitis is followed by new bone formation, so inflamed ligament attachments ossify into syndesmophytes and the spine fuses, unlike the erosive, bone-losing course of RA. Inflammatory back pain improves with movement and worsens with rest, which separates it from mechanical back pain. Gut and genitourinary infections can trigger the same joint and eye inflammation in susceptible people, which is the basis of reactive arthritis.

points: Purine breakdown: hypoxanthine to xanthine to uric acid, both steps by xanthine oxidase
Underexcretion causes most gout: kidney disease, thiazide and loop diuretics, alcohol, low-dose aspirin
Overproduction: Lesch-Nyhan (HGPRT deficiency), tumor lysis, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency
Acute gout: hot, red first MTP (podagra) after alcohol or a purine-rich meal
Chronic gout: tophi, punched-out erosions with overhanging edges, uric acid kidney stones
Pseudogout: calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the knee or wrist, chondrocalcinosis; linked to hyperparathyroidism and hemochromatosis
notes.why: Humans lack uricase, so urate is the end product of purine breakdown and serum levels sit close to their solubility limit; crystals form when concentration rises or temperature falls, as in the cool first MTP joint. About two thirds of urate is excreted by the kidney, so reduced filtration, or drugs and organic acids that cut tubular urate excretion (diuretics, low-dose aspirin, and lactate from alcohol), raises the level. Overproduction comes from high cell turnover or failed purine salvage: without HGPRT, hypoxanthine and guanine are degraded and unused PRPP drives more de novo purine synthesis. Pseudogout crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent, while urate crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.

points: Dermatomyositis: complement-mediated capillary injury, perifascicular atrophy, heliotrope rash, Gottron papules; screen for internal cancer
Polymyositis: endomysial CD8 T cells invading muscle fibers, no rash
Both: symmetric proximal weakness, high CK, myofiber necrosis; anti-Jo-1 marks interstitial lung disease risk
Polymyalgia rheumatica: adults over 50 with shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, high ESR, normal CK and strength
PMR travels with giant cell arteritis; new headache, jaw claudication, or visual change signals risk of vision loss
Steroid myopathy: proximal weakness with normal CK and type II fiber atrophy without inflammation
notes.why: The inflammatory myopathies differ in what the immune system attacks. In dermatomyositis, complement injures endomysial capillaries, and capillary loss starves fibers at the edge of each fascicle, producing perifascicular atrophy; in polymyositis, muscle fibers express MHC class I and CD8 T cells kill them directly. Both destroy fibers and release CK, whereas PMR inflames bursae and synovium around the shoulders and hips and leaves muscle intact, so CK and strength are normal while ESR is high. PMR and giant cell arteritis share an IL-6-driven inflammatory picture and often occur in the same patient.

points: Prepatellar bursitis from kneeling; olecranon bursitis from leaning or trauma; subacromial and trochanteric from overuse
Septic bursitis (most often Staphylococcus aureus) follows a skin break, most often prepatellar or olecranon
Tendinopathy (tendinosis): overuse causes collagen disorganization and neovascularization with few inflammatory cells
Lateral epicondylitis: extensor carpi radialis brevis origin; medial epicondylitis: common flexor-pronator origin
Supraspinatus impingement: painful arc from about 60 to 120 degrees of abduction
De Quervain tenosynovitis: abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, positive Finkelstein test
Plantar fasciitis: heel pain with first morning steps; fluoroquinolones raise Achilles tendinopathy and rupture risk
notes.why: Bursae are synovial-lined sacs that reduce friction, so repeated pressure inflames them, and the superficial bursae over the knee and elbow lie close to skin breaks where bacteria enter. Chronic tendinopathy is a failed healing response with few inflammatory cells: repeated microtears outpace repair, leaving disorganized collagen, increased ground substance, and ingrowth of vessels and nerves. Impingement pain is felt mid-arc because the supraspinatus tendon passes under the acromion and coracoacromial arch between about 60 and 120 degrees of abduction. Fluoroquinolones appear to injure tenocytes and tendon matrix, which raises the risk of Achilles tendinopathy and rupture.

notes.h: Fibromyalgia, JIA, and other soft tissue
points: Fibromyalgia: central pain sensitization; widespread pain for at least 3 months, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, mostly women
Fibromyalgia labs are normal: ESR, CRP, and CK
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: arthritis before age 16 lasting at least 6 weeks
Oligoarticular JIA: young girls, ANA positive, silent anterior uveitis; systemic JIA: daily spiking fever and salmon-colored rash
Adhesive capsulitis: capsular inflammation and fibrosis, loss of both active and passive shoulder motion, linked to diabetes
Ganglion cyst: myxoid degeneration near a joint capsule or tendon sheath, often dorsal wrist, no true lining
notes.why: Fibromyalgia is a disorder of pain processing in which central sensitization amplifies signals from normal tissue, so pain is widespread while ESR, CRP, and CK stay normal. Oligoarticular JIA links ANA positivity to chronic anterior uveitis that causes no pain or redness, so children need regular slit-lamp screening to prevent vision loss. In adhesive capsulitis, the capsule thickens and contracts, mechanically limiting passive as well as active motion, which separates it from rotator cuff disease where passive motion is preserved. A ganglion is filled with mucinous fluid and walled by compressed connective tissue with no synovial lining, which makes it a pseudocyst.
